source.title: The Model Shape Behind Scaling Laws: A Gradient Superposition Perspective
source.authors: Wen-Jie Sun; Jin-Ning Yang; Shuai Zhang; Meng-Nan Du

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly reproduces a sparse-reconstruction toy-model double-descent experiment and measures test reconstruction loss across training-sample sizes. It also adds a Gaussian minimum-norm regression sample-size sweep.
record.gate_note: The sparse-reconstruction and Gaussian-regression sample-size outcomes are included. The paper also reports AGOP norms, language-model shape/loss associations, and local perturbation results; these do not directly measure the claim versions about test-error double descent, so they are not separate rows. Cited prior-work findings are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces the Henighan et al. sparse-reconstruction toy double descent, a sample-size sweep of test loss in a tied ReLU autoencoder. It also runs a Gaussian minimum-norm regression sample-size sweep at noise 0 and 0.3. Both report test error versus training-set size, so they bear on V3, and the noise comparison bears on V6. Neither setting matches the originals' deep-network setups, so this is a new setting (T3). The paper's main aim is the AGOP observable, but the loss curves themselves are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The authors' headline conclusion is about language-model shape: among validation-selected depth-width shapes, and within budgets from 10M to 50M, lower loss accompanies lower AGOP norm. They read effective parameter allocation as reducing error-response amplification. The double-descent experiments serve as a controlled mechanism: the toy peak is a shared loss/AGOP peak not identified with interpolation, and in noisy min-norm regression a fitted-noise term drives both risk and AGOP, with the singularity absent without noise.
record.recipe_differences: The sparse-reconstruction experiment is described as a reproduction of Anthropic’s toy-model double-descent experiment, with its stated setup and sample-size sweep. The paper additionally studies Gaussian minimum-norm regression and language-model architecture shapes; those are not replications of the original intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The regression peak depends on training noise: the paper reports it for noise standard deviation 0.3 and its absence in the noiseless control. Sparse-reconstruction dataset seeds vary with sample size; the five initialization seeds share each size’s train and test datasets, so initialization SEM does not quantify data-resampling uncertainty.

fits_no_version.finding: The Frobenius norm of the input AGOP tracks toy test loss across the full sample sweep, sharing the n=500 peak (r=0.979, affine fit R²=0.958). In regression, AGOP norm and risk share the same fitted-noise term and singularity at n=p.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A functional input-sensitivity norm (AGOP) co-varies with test error along a sample-wise double-descent curve and peaks at the same sample size.

record.problems: The sparse-reconstruction peak is not shown to be at exact interpolation, and its initialization SEM does not measure dataset-resampling uncertainty. The Gaussian-regression figure gives 10–90% intervals, but numeric bounds are not stated in the text. The Gaussian comparison reports noise levels 0 and 0.3; although 0.1 is listed in the protocol, no corresponding results are reported in the included table or figures.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant outcome rows omitted. The paper’s language-model shape/loss scans and local perturbation audit concern associations or sensitivity under architecture changes, not the claim’s specified double-descent versions.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; architecture is fixed in both double-descent experiments.
No test error tracked over training epochs.
No capacity sweep past interpolation across model classes; only sample size varies.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples. AGOP tracks loss only along the sample axis.
Multiple or triple peaks and optimally tuned regularization are not tested. Noise σ=0.1 is listed in the protocol but not reported, and noise is not varied in the toy autoencoder.
No reparameterisation by effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Toy training loss at each n. At the n=500 test-loss peak, train loss is 0.9606, far from zero, so the peak is not at interpolation.
Matched training-mean/bias-only predictor (zero AGOP) loss at every n. The network is above it from n=1946 on, e.g. 0.993247 vs 0.992437 at n=40000.
Frozen-signal noise-fitting regression (k=128, σ=0.3): median loss peaks at 51.6 at n=128 and falls on either side.
Noise σ=0.1 regression results are listed in the protocol but not reported.

record.verdict_notes: Henighan et al.'s toy model is not an original source, so verdicts are allowed. The reader's row states treated decreases before the peak as 'partial' and negligible late fluctuations as partial or observed; these are corrected above. Toy SEM is over initialisations only, since datasets are shared, so small toy differences cannot be judged against data-resampling noise. The regression setting is linear, so its V3 support is outside deep networks. Language-model shape scans and the perturbation audit do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No controlled sweep of deep-network model size through an interpolation threshold testing the stated fall-rise-fall test-error curve.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.

The sparse-autoencoder peak is not identified as an exact interpolation threshold; the Gaussian regression experiment measures clean population risk rather than empirical test error. The paper does not test other data regimes or models beyond those reported.
The study does not test capacity-wise double descent across model classes. The regression sweep varies sample size, not model capacity.
AGOP norm is measured alongside loss, but the study does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The regression experiment compares zero noise with nonzero Gaussian noise. Multiple/triple peaks and optimally tuned regularization are not tested; noise is not varied in the sparse-reconstruction experiment.
No test of whether counting an appropriate effective number of parameters converts a second-descent curve into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
